name: dummy
intent: Satisfy a required parameter slot with the language's absent or unit value - or a minimal do-nothing stand-in - when the exercised path never reads it, so a test does not have to build a real collaborator or a stub for an input that cannot influence the outcome.
problem: A method or constructor the test must call declares a parameter the code path under test never reads: a collaborator, logger, locale, clock, policy, user-data pointer or callback. The argument cannot simply be dropped, because the signature requires it, a framework calls back with it, or the type system has no notion of 'no value'. Test authors then construct the real depended-on component (slow, unavailable, side-effecting), copy a stub for a call nobody makes, or pass an absent value while the assumption 'this path never touches it' stays undocumented and unverified.
context: Unit tests that isolate a system under test behind a substitutable-dependency seam, where one argument of a call is mandatory but irrelevant to the behaviour being exercised. It is the cheapest member of the Test Double family: no behaviour, no configuration, no expectations, and it stays valid exactly as long as the exercised path does not read the parameter. The pattern applies in every language, but its cost differs sharply - from a free undefined in JavaScript to a hand-written do-nothing callback in C - and the risk is the same everywhere: the validity of the claim is never checked by the test itself.
benefits: Nothing is implemented: no double class, no canned answers, no expectations - the placeholder is the language's absent or unit value, or a one-line no-op where a value is mandatory.
Fixture setup shrinks: the test stops constructing, wiring and persisting a real collaborator that the assertion does not depend on, which keeps the test small and fast.
There is less room for drift than with any other double: a placeholder that is never read cannot diverge from the behaviour of the real depended-on component.
It documents an assumption in place: passing a placeholder at a call site says which parameter this path ignores, information a reader would otherwise have to reconstruct from production code.
It keeps the double budget focused: only the collaborators that carry the behaviour under test need Stubs, Spies, Mocks or Fakes.
It removes the temptation to test through a collaborator that is irrelevant here, which is a common source of slow, brittle, overspecified tests.
tradeoffs: 'Unused on this path' is an unverified claim: nothing in the test checks it, so the day the path starts reading the parameter the test fails as a null/None dereference, a panic or a zero-value comparison deep inside the SUT rather than as a clear contract violation.

An auto-answering double used as a placeholder hides that change completely: an unspec'd mock accepts any member and returns defaults, so a parameter that is now read keeps the suite green with fabricated data.

In null-hostile type systems the placeholder costs an escape hatch - a cast, a null-forgiving operator, an empty conformance - and those escapes also silence genuine type errors in the same expression.

Where the language has no absent value the pattern is not free: a real instance must be fabricated (a default-constructed object, a no-op trait implementation, an empty anonymous class), which is the hand-written code the pattern was supposed to avoid.
Like every Test Double it exercises the SUT in a configuration different from production, so at least one test must run against real collaborators to catch drift.
A placeholder in an argument list is also a signature smell: a parameter that every path ignores should be removed, defaulted or modelled as absence rather than paid for in every test.
In dynamically typed languages the placeholder is invisible to the compiler and to the reader's tools, so nothing at all stands between a wrong choice and a failure inside the system under test.

participants.responsibility: The placeholder value itself - an absent or unit value, a default-constructed instance or a do-nothing implementation. It carries no behaviour, is never configured and must never be read.

The position in the signature (constructor argument, method parameter, framework callback argument, generic type parameter) that forces the call to supply something although the exercised path ignores it.
Chooses the cheapest placeholder the language and the declared type allow, supplies it at the call site, and thereby states that the path under test does not depend on this input.
The code being exercised; it must not read the placeholder. That assumption makes the dummy valid and is the pattern's main risk, because nothing in the test enforces it.

use_cases: Constructing the system under test when its constructor demands a collaborator the exercised path never calls (logger, audit sink, metrics client, second repository).

Framework and library callbacks with fixed signatures: a scheduled task that receives a cancellation token it never observes, a UI handler that ignores its event argument, a visitor method that takes a context object it does not inspect.

Generically constrained code that must be instantiated with a type or value of no interest, where the language's unit type is the canonical placeholder (() and PhantomData in Rust, std::monostate in C++, akka.NotUsed in Scala).
APIs with unused user-data arguments: C callbacks taking a void *ctx, comparators taking a data pointer, listener registration passing an options object.
A narrow path through a wide collaborator interface: the interface has twenty members and the path calls none of them, so a placeholder is cheaper and more honest than implementing the interface.
Localisation, clock and policy parameters on a path that never reads them, such as a formatter test that exercises only the numeric branch.

Go table-driven tests where sub-tests call a shared helper that accepts an interface satisfied by nil: the sub-test exercises a path that never invokes the store, repository, or logger, so nil is the cheapest and most honest stand-in.

Rust generic code parameterised over a type context that is never read — PhantomData<()> in a generic struct signals 'this type is stored for variance only' and serves as a zero-cost compile-time dummy for the generic parameter.

TypeScript / React component props that include optional callbacks (onSuccess, onError) for paths the test does not exercise: passing undefined for those props is idiomatic and documents exactly which hooks the exercised behaviour does not trigger.

Framework lifecycle hooks with fixed signatures: Angular ngOnDestroy, useEffect cleanup in React, Flask teardown_request — these receive a parameter the handler never reads for the exercised path, so null/undefined satisfies the signature without inducing side effects.

Generically constrained code that must be instantiated with a type or value of no interest where the language's unit type is the canonical placeholder: std::monostate in C++, akka.NotUsed in Scala, NotUsed in Akka, () in Rust.

A callback argument in a higher-order function where the composed function never invokes the callback on the exercised path: pass null or undefined as the dummy callback to keep the test focused on the composed behaviour without wiring a no-op function.

Akka Streams placeholder materialized value: operators that produce no control panel or completion handle materialize akka.NotUsed, which Akka 2.4 deliberately migrated to from Unit/BoxedUnit so 'this generic slot carries no value' is expressible in both Scala and Java APIs.

C++ std::variant<std::monostate, T>: when the real alternative is not default-constructible, std::monostate is the standard library's canonical placeholder giving the variant a well-defined 'no value yet' default state that query code can test for instead of fabricating a value.

Rust PhantomData<T> in a generic struct that never actually stores a T - a zero-sized dummy that keeps the compiler's ownership, variance and drop-check reasoning honest for a generic parameter the runtime code never reads.
avoid_when: The exercised path reads the parameter, even on a single branch: that calls for a Stub, a Fake or the real collaborator, not a placeholder.
The test must observe what the collaborator received: use a Spy, Mock or Recording Fake, because a placeholder that is never read records nothing.
The placeholder would have to absorb calls the assertion depends on, or stand in for the component under test - promote it to a configurable double instead.
The signature can express absence itself: an optional or defaulted parameter, an overload, or a nullable/Option type means 'pass nothing', which is better than 'pass a placeholder'.
Every path ignores the parameter: delete or default it in the production signature rather than shelling out a dummy in every test.
A cheap working implementation is what the test actually needs (in-memory repository, fake clock): a Fake carries the behaviour and stays honest about it.
anti_patterns: Placeholder in a path that does read the parameter: the test then pins a null dereference, a panic or a fabricated default instead of the behaviour it means to verify.
Unspec'd auto-double used as a dummy: an unconfigured mock or double accepts every member, so interface drift and newly used parameters stay invisible and the test passes vacuously.
Placeholder swapped in for the component under test, so the double replaces the very collaborator whose behaviour the test claims to verify.

Null-escaping everywhere: non-null assertions, casts and null-forgiving operators sprinkled through tests (and sometimes production) just to thread placeholders through signatures, which also masks real nullability defects.
Placeholder as a blanket default: every test constructs a heavy 'just in case' object or a catch-all double because nobody checked which parameters the exercised paths actually read.
design_principles: Least effort / YAGNI: supply the smallest thing that satisfies the signature; build behaviour only for inputs the test actually depends on.
Explicitness: a placeholder states which inputs the exercised path ignores, making an assumption of the test visible in the test itself.
Single responsibility: dummies carry no behaviour - control points are Stubs, observation points are Spies and Mocks, working implementations are Fakes.
Substitutability: the placeholder must stay type-compatible with the declared parameter type; a cast that erases the type is accumulated debt, not a solution.
Separation of concerns: test infrastructure (which collaborator matters here) stays distinct from production semantics (which parameters the API has).
best_practices: Prefer the language's absent or unit value (null, nil, None, undefined, nullptr, ()) or a default-constructed instance; write code only when the declared type forces it.
Make the assumption visible: name the placeholder ('unusedClock') or comment the call site, so a later failure is diagnosed as 'this path changed' rather than as flakiness.
Construct placeholders inline at the call site; never park them in shared fixtures or module-level state, where they become cross-test state.
When a do-nothing implementation is unavoidable, decide deliberately whether it should fail loudly on use (pinning the assumption) or stay inert (merely satisfying the signature).
Do not let a toolkit's auto-answering double stand in for a dummy: if a mock is used, spec it against the real interface so removed members fail, and keep the expectation that it is never called.
Keep at least one test per behaviour that runs against the real collaborator or a Fake, so the paths assumed to be unused are exercised somewhere.
When a parameter turns out to be unused on every path, change the production signature (remove, default or model absence) instead of paying for a placeholder in every test.

Name the assumption explicitly: label the placeholder ('unusedClock', 'ignoredNotifier') or add a comment at the call site so the next reader understands why null is being passed, and so a future 'Parameter is read' failure is diagnosed as a code-change symptom rather than test flakiness.

Prefer the language's native absent value (null, nil, None, undefined, nullptr, ()) over a hand-rolled do-nothing class when the type system permits it — it costs nothing and makes the placeholder intention unmistakable.

When a do-nothing implementation is unavoidable, prefer one that fails loudly on first use (throws, panics, logs a fatal) rather than a silent one — a hard failure pinpoints the exact moment the exercised path started reading a parameter it previously ignored, turning a silent correctness drift into an immediate, actionable signal.

Keep dummy definitions local to the test or the test file; never park them in shared module-level variables or fixtures, because shared mutable state between tests is a source of non-deterministic failures.

Add a single integration test per behaviour that runs against the real collaborator (or a Fake) so that any path that started reading a previously-unused parameter is caught by the test suite even if the unit test stays green.

Treat a parameter that every code path ignores as a signature smell: it should be removed, made optional, or modelled as explicit absence in the production API rather than paid for as a dummy in every test.

In Rust, the unit type () is the canonical dummy; in Go, nil satisfies most interfaces and is idiomatic when the exercised path provably does not call the method; in TypeScript, undefined is the cheapest placeholder — do not fabricate an object when the language already offers a free absent value.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (Addison-Wesley, 2007) - Test Double (Chapter 23, p. 522) and the Dummy Object variation (p. 526): the placeholder 'may be as simple as a null object reference, an instance of the Object class, or an instance of a Pseudo-Object', and Figure 23.2 records that Dummy Objects have no implementation. The pattern's own write-up (p. 728) carries the aliases Dummy Parameter, Dummy Value, Placeholder, Dummy Argument and Dummy Attribute.

Martin Fowler. TestDouble. (2006) — Fowler's bliki entry introducing the Test Double umbrella term from Meszaros's vocabulary, defining Dummy as 'passed around but never actually used, usually just to fill parameter lists.'

kexugit. Unit Testing: Exploring the Continuum of Test Doubles. (2007) — MSDN Magazine article presenting test doubles as a continuum rather than discrete types, noting that 'dummies' inhabit one extreme with absolutely no implementation, and that the boundaries between dummy/stub/spy are intentionally blurred in practice.

Tobias Duereschmid. Test Doubles — SE Book. (2025) — Living book chapter covering the Meszaros taxonomy with a decision table: Dummy is the lightest double (fills a parameter slot, never used) and the minimum-viable-double rule — escalate only when the test needs the double to do something.

Jeff Atwood. Test Doubles: A Taxonomy of Pretend Objects. (2007) — Coding Horror post popularising Fowler's article and the Meszaros vocabulary: Dummy, Stub, Fake, Mock — with the observation that Dummy is the simplest test double.

Chris Ammerman. A Taxonomy of Test Doubles. (2011) — Contrasts the Meszaros/Fowler vocabulary with earlier record/replay mock frameworks; notes that 'dummy' is probably the most common test double and is most efficiently created using a mock framework even when no behaviour is configured.

Software Patterns Lexicon. Null Object Pattern in Go. (2026) — Distinguishes Null Object (USED by SUT, implements interface with no-op behaviour) from Dummy (never used by SUT); emphasises 'Null Object is intentionally boring' and that Null Objects are not substitutes for assertions.

Syarif. Test Doubles in Go Without a Mocking Framework: 4 Patterns. (2026) — Shows that Go dummies are typically plain structs with nil interfaces when the exercised path does not read the dependency; contrasts hand-rolled stubs, configurable fakes, and httptest-backed adapters.
